recommendation_tables.title: Table 4 New recommendations

rows.recommendation: Although the concept of the Pregnancy Heart Team was previously part of the general principles, it has now been given its own dedicated section, which covers all aspects from pre-conception through to the postpartum period.

A discussion by the Pregnancy Heart Team about the high risk of maternal mortality or morbidity and the related high foetal risk is recommended for women with mWHO 2.0 class IV conditions, including a shared decision-making process for pregnancy termination, involving psychological support.
It is recommended that women with CVD of mWHO 2.0 class II–III and above are evaluated and managed by a Pregnancy Heart Team from pre-pregnancy onwards through pregnancy and post-partum.

Measurement of BNP and NT-proBNP levels should be considered prior to pregnancy in women with HF of any aetiology, including previous PPCM, cardiomyopathy, ACHD, and PAH, and be monitored during pregnancy according to the underlying disorder and in case of new-onset or worsening symptoms.

Given the importance of medication use throughout this document, this section has been brought forward and revised. The former comprehensive medication table has been moved to the Supplementary data online, and we provide a summary figure (Figure 6) listing the (contra)indicated medications.
This section has been expanded since 2018 for advice in specific cardiomyopathies and primary arrhythmias.

Vaginal delivery is recommended in most women with CMPs, unless there are obstetric indications for caesarean section, severe HF (EF <30% and/or NYHA class III/IV), uncontrolled arrhythmias, or severe outflow obstruction (≥50 mmHg) in women with HCM, or in women presenting in labour on VKAs.
In women with DCM and worsening of EF during pregnancy, counselling on the risk of recurrence during a subsequent pregnancy is recommended in all cases, even after recovery of LV function.

It is recommended that women with HCM with symptomatic LV dysfunction (EF <50%) and or severe LVOTO (≥50 mmHg) wishing to become pregnant are counselled by the Pregnancy Heart Team regarding the high risk of pregnancy-related adverse events.
Myosin inhibitors are not recommended in women during pregnancy due to lack of safety data.

rows.recommendation: Beta-blockers, with pre-pregnancy dose and with nadolol and propranolol as drugs of choice, are recommended during pregnancy in women with LQTS.
It is recommended to continue beta-blocker therapy during lactation in women with LQTS to reduce arrhythmic risk.

Pre-pregnancy dose beta-blockers of nadolol or propranolol is recommended in patients with LQT2, particularly in the post-partum period, which represents a high-risk period for life-threatening arrhythmias.
Beta-blockers, with pre-pregnancy dose and with nadolol and propranolol as drugs of choice, are recommended during pregnancy and lactation in women with CPVT.
Flecainide, in addition to beta-blockers, is recommended in women with CPVT who experience cardiac events, such as syncope, VT, or cardiac arrest during pregnancy.

rows.recommendation: Genetic counselling and testing should be considered in women with PPCM.

recommendation_tables.title: Pregnancy in women with aortopathies

rows.recommendation: It is recommended that women with a history of aortic dissection or ‑surgery have pre-pregnancy counselling about the high risk by an extended Pregnancy Heart Team considering the presence and type of genetic variant, aortic morphology, growth rate, and aetiology of aortic dissection.

recommendation_tables.title: Pregnancy in women with known congenital heart disease

rows.recommendation: It is recommended that all women with Fontan circulation who wish to become pregnant receive counselling from the Pregnancy Heart Team regarding the high risk of pregnancy-related adverse events.

recommendation_tables.title: Pregnancy in women with pulmonary arterial hypertension

rows.recommendation: It is recommended that women of childbearing potential with PAH wishing to become pregnant are counselled by a multidisciplinary team regarding the very high risk of pregnancy-related adverse events, encouraging a shared decision-making process about whether to become pregnant.

recommendation_tables.title: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy and post-partum

rows.recommendation: In pregnant women or women in the post-partum period with suspicion of venous thromboembolism (VTE) [deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and/or PE], an immediate formal diagnostic assessment with validated methods is recommended and should not be postponed.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for coronary artery disease and pregnancy

rows.recommendation: In pregnant women with chest pain, it is recommended to exclude life-threatening cardiovascular conditions, including PE, ACS (including SCAD), and acute aortic syndrome.

The duration of DAPT (aspirin and clopidogrel) in pregnant women undergoing coronary stent implantation is recommended to be the same as in non-pregnant women, with an individual approach considering ischaemic risk and delivery-related bleeding risks.
Continuation of statins may be considered during pregnancy in women with established ASCVD.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for hypertensive disorders and pregnancy

rows.recommendation: It is recommended to aim for systolic BP <140 mmHg and diastolic BP <90 mmHg in pregnant women.

In severe hypertension, drug treatment with i.v. labetalol, urapidil, nicardipine, or oral short acting nifedipine or methyldopa is recommended for acute reduction in blood pressure. Intravenous hydralazine is a second-line option.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for supraventricular tachycardia and pregnancy

rows.recommendation: Therapeutic anticoagulation with LMWH is recommended for pregnant women with persistent or permanent AF at elevated thromboembolic risk.
Flecainide, in addition to beta-blockers, should be considered for long-term AF rhythm control in pregnancy.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation for ventricular tachycardia, device implantation and catheter ablation and pregnancy

rows.recommendation: When performing catheter ablation during pregnancy, the use of non-fluoroscopic mapping and navigation systems should be considered.

content.narrative_summary: The epidemiology section describes a rising number of pregnancies complicated by acquired, congenital, or inherited cardiovascular disease (CVD) in high-income countries, linked to factors such as higher maternal age and more women with congenital heart disease reaching childbearing age. Maternal CVD is now a leading cause of non-obstetric mortality, accounting for up to 33% of pregnancy-related deaths, with adverse neonatal outcomes in about 25% and increased long-term CVD risk in offspring. The physiology section outlines cardiovascular adaptations in pregnancy, noting increased metabolic demands and early gestational rises in stroke volume and cardiac output.

recommendation_tables.title: Section 8. Recommendations for aortopathies, cardiac surgery, and pregnancy

rows.recommendation: Pregnancy is not recommended in patients with vascular Ehlers–Danlos syndrome.

It is recommended that women with vascular Ehlers–Danlos syndrome wishing to become pregnant are counselled regarding the very high risk of pregnancy-related adverse events by a multidisciplinary team, considering family history, genetic variant, and previous vascular events.
Beta-blocker therapy throughout pregnancy should be considered in women with Marfan syndrome and other heritable thoracic aortic diseases.
Beta-blocker therapy throughout pregnancy and in the post-partum period is recommended in women with MFS and other HTADs.

recommendation_tables.title: Section 9. Recommendations for congenital heart disease and pregnancy

rows.recommendation: Patients with a systemic right ventricle (Mustard/Senning or congenitally corrected TGA), in NYHA class III/IV, systemic ventricular dysfunction (EF <40%), or severe TR should be advised against pregnancy.

It is recommended that women with a systemic RV (Mustard/Senning or congenitally corrected TGA), in NYHA class III/IV, systemic ventricular dysfunction (EF <40%), or severe TR wishing to become pregnant are counselled by the Pregnancy Heart Team regarding the high risk of pregnancy-related adverse events.

recommendation_tables.title: Section 12. Recommendations for acquired heart disease and pregnancy

rows.recommendation: An invasive management strategy should be considered for NSTE ACS with high-risk criteria.
It is recommended to manage pregnant women with ACS in the same way as non-pregnant women, including diagnostic investigations and interventions.
Catheter ablation with electro-anatomical systems should be considered in experienced centres in cases of drug-refractory and poorly tolerated SVT.
Catheter ablation may be considered in pregnant women with recurrent, long symptomatic SVT or with contraindications to pharmacological therapies.
Balloon aortic valvuloplasty should be considered during pregnancy in patients with severe aortic stenosis and severe symptoms.
In very selected symptomatic pregnant women with severe aortic stenosis not responding to medical therapy, non-surgical options such as balloon valvuloplasty or TAVI may be considered.
A bioprosthesis should be considered in young women contemplating pregnancy.
A bioprosthetic valve is recommended (over a mechanical valve) in young women contemplating pregnancy requiring a valve prosthesis.

During the second and third trimesters, LMWH with anti-factor Xa level monitoring and dose adjustment (see separate recommendations) may be considered in women who need a high dose of VKA after patient information and consent.
During the second and third trimesters until the 36th week, continuing VKAs should be considered in women with prosthetic heart valves at higher risk of thrombosis.

content.narrative_summary: Following pregnancy, cardiac output (CO) increases by 30%–50%, and heart rate increases by 10–20 beats per minute. Peripheral vascular resistance decreases by 20%–50%. Left and right atrial and ventricular diameters and volumes increase while ventricular function remains preserved. Blood pressure and CO rise during labour, then after delivery CO drops rapidly to approximately 15%–25% above normal and gradually returns to pre-pregnancy levels over the next 3–4 weeks, reaching baseline by around 6 weeks post-partum. In women with pre-existing heart disease, ventricular adaptation may be suboptimal, leading to heart failure and atrial or ventricular tachyarrhythmias. The haemodynamic and hormonal changes of pregnancy increase the risk of aortic dissection in those with aortopathy. Pregnancy is a hypercoagulable state with increased thromboembolism risk. Enhanced gastrointestinal-hepatic metabolism, raised liver enzyme activity, increased glomerular filtration rate, expanded plasma volume, altered protein binding, and reduced serum albumin all contribute to changes in drug pharmacokinetics.

content.narrative_summary: The narrative discusses the management of women with cardiovascular disease (CVD) seeking reproductive treatment, emphasising that they should not be denied treatment without multidisciplinary evaluation by a Pregnancy Heart Team. It outlines the additional pro-thrombotic risks of assisted reproduction, notably ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome and venous thromboembolism (VTE), and advises individual VTE risk assessment. Strategies to mitigate ovarian hyperstimulation risk include careful cycle monitoring with low-dose follicle-stimulating hormone and gonadotropin-releasing hormone antagonist. Single-embryo transfer is strongly recommended due to higher cardiovascular and maternal-fetal complications associated with multiple gestations. Women with mWHO 2.0 class III conditions or those on anticoagulation have very high superovulation risks and should undergo full pre-pregnancy assessment by a Pregnancy Heart Team.

rows.recommendation: It is recommended to perform a risk assessment in all women with CVD of childbearing age using the mWHO 2.0 classification.

A discussion by the Pregnancy Heart Team about the high risk of maternal mortality or morbidity and the related high foetal risk is recommended for women with mWHO 2.0 class IV conditions, including a shared decision-making process for pregnancy termination, involving psychological support.
It is recommended that women with CVD of mWHO 2.0 class II–III and above are evaluated and managed by a Pregnancy Heart Team from pre-pregnancy onwards through pregnancy and post-partum.

It is recommended that women with CVD of mWHO 2.0 class II and above, or those at risk of developing CVD, receive individualized advice to determine the most suitable contraception method, including emergency contraception.
Progestin-only treatment, contraceptive implants, and/or levonorgestrel IUDs should be considered when there is any risk of thromboembolic events.

Assessment by a clinical geneticist prior to pregnancy is recommended in women fulfilling diagnostic criteria for inherited cardiovascular disease to guide risk stratification and pre-natal genetic testing.

Pre-conception genetic counselling is recommended in couples with heritable CVD, whether genetic testing is being considered or not. It is recommended that this counselling is provided by an appropriately trained healthcare professional within a multidisciplinary team that offers psychological support and education to encourage decision-making.
It is recommended that single embryo transfer is performed in women with CVD.
It is recommended to offer women with CVD access to termination of pregnancy that is tailored to their cardiac condition to minimize the risks of the procedure.

section_headings: 4.3.5.2. Computed tomography and nuclear medicine imaging
content.narrative_summary: This section reviews cardiovascular diagnostic tools in pregnancy, including expected ECG changes (e.g., increased heart rate, leftward QRS axis shift, T-wave inversions) and indications for long-term monitoring devices. Transthoracic echocardiography is affirmed as first-line imaging, with discussion of safety concerns around contrast agents, speckle-tracking, and transoesophageal approaches. Submaximal exercise testing is discussed for suspected CVD, noting lack of evidence for increased miscarriage risk and avoidance of pharmacologic stress. Natriuretic peptides (BNP, NT-proBNP) are highlighted for their negative predictive value. The risks of fetal ionizing radiation are outlined, with ALARA principles for chest radiography, guidance on ultrasound limitations, and estimated radiation doses for CT and nuclear medicine procedures.

content.narrative_summary: Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is a life-threatening form of heart failure with reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (<45%) occurring in the peripartum period or months after delivery. Incidence varies by region, with 1–4/1000 births in the United States and 10/1000 in northern Nigeria. Worldwide, PPCM complicates about 1 in 2000 births. Diagnosis is by exclusion and requires urgent management. Recent data suggest a “multiple hit” theory involving genetic and environmental factors; up to 15% of women with PPCM carry truncating variants in TTN, FLNC, BAG3, or DSP. Mechanisms may include inflammation, oxidative stress, and an anti-angiogenic 16 kDa prolactin fragment causing endothelial dysfunction. Bromocriptine has emerged as a potential targeted therapy. Diagnosis should include ECG, natriuretic peptides, and echocardiography, with management by a Pregnancy Heart Team and avoidance of teratogenic heart failure medications.

content.narrative_summary: Prophylactic cardiac surgery in women planning pregnancy is more common than urgent or emergency surgery. Aortic surgery, including for aortic and mitral valve disease, carries risks such as prosthetic valve thrombosis and endocarditis. Surgery with extracorporeal circulation and cardioplegic arrest is individualized. A meta-analysis reported a 7.3% maternal mortality rate consistent across trimesters, with no difference if caesarean was performed. Overall foetal mortality was 26.5%, lowest in the third trimester (10.3%). Caesarean before surgery reduces foetal mortality and should be based on foetal viability and level of neonatal care rather than gestational age. Hypothermic distal circulatory arrest increases foetal mortality.

rows.recommendation: It is recommended that women with aortic disease have counselling about the risk of aortic dissection in pregnancy and the post-partum period.

It is recommended that women with a history of aortic dissection or -surgery have pre-pregnancy counselling about the high risk by an extended Pregnancy Heart Team considering the presence and type of genetic variant, aortic morphology, growth rate, and aetiology of aortic dissection.

It is recommended that women with vascular Ehlers–Danlos syndrome wishing to become pregnant are counselled regarding the very high risk of pregnancy-related adverse events by a multidisciplinary team, considering family history, genetic variant, and previous vascular events.
Imaging of the entire aorta (CT or CMR) is recommended before pregnancy in women with known or suspected aortic disease.

In women with aortic dilatation related to BAV, imaging (with TTE, and CMR/CT if needed) of the aortic root, ascending aorta, and descending aorta (to rule out coarctation) is recommended before pregnancy.
In women with low-risk aortic disease (mWHO 2.0 classes II and II–III), one-time echocardiographic imaging between 20 and 30 weeks of gestation and imaging at 6 months post-partum is recommended.

In women with moderate to high-risk aortic disease (mWHO 2.0 classes III and IV), repeated echocardiographic imaging every 4–12 weeks (depending on diagnosis and severity of dilatation) is recommended during pregnancy and until 6 months post-partum.
CMR (without gadolinium) imaging of the entire aorta is recommended in pregnant women at risk of or with known aortic dilatation who have not had recent pre-pregnancy cross sectional imaging.
When a woman with known aortic dilatation, history of dissection, or P/L/P variant associated with aortic disease becomes pregnant, strict and individualized BP control is recommended.
Beta-blocker therapy throughout pregnancy and in the post-partum period is recommended in women with MFS and other HTADs.
Celiprolol is recommended in women with vascular Ehlers–Danlos syndrome during pregnancy and lactation.

It is recommended that indications for pre-pregnancy aortic root and/or ascending aortic surgery are guided by aortic morphology, underlying pathology, family history, genetic variant, previous vascular events, and patient’s preference.
It is recommended that centres managing pregnancies in women with moderate to high-risk aortic disease (mWHO 2.0 class III/IV) can provide cardiovascular surgery in case of peripartum adverse events.
In women with MFS and aortic root diameters >45 mm, surgery before pregnancy is recommended.
In women with LDS with P/L/P variants in TGFBR1, TGFBR2, and aortic root diameters ≥45 mm, surgery before pregnancy is recommended.

content.narrative_summary: Congenital heart disease (CHD) affects approximately 0.8–0.9% of live births, with significant geographical variation. Advances in paediatric care have increased the number of adults with CHD, making it a common cardiovascular condition in pregnancy. section_headings: 10. Pregnancy in women with pulmonary arterial hypertension
content.narrative_summary: Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is defined as mean pulmonary arterial pressure >20 mmHg and pre-capillary PAH as pulmonary vascular resistance >2 Wood units with wedge pressure ≤15 mmHg. Untreated idiopathic PAH has a median survival of 2.8 years, extended beyond 7 years with therapy. PAH predominates in women, including those of childbearing age; management requires a Pregnancy Heart Team and PH expert across the ante-, peri- and postpartum periods. Maternal and foetal risks are higher in moderate-to-severe and Eisenmenger-type PAH; all women should be counselled on risks, contraception and potential pregnancy termination. Management includes bed rest, avoidance of additional risks, targeted PAH therapy optimization with safe agents (PDE5 inhibitors, prostacyclin analogues), discontinuation of teratogenic agents (ERAs, riociguat, selexipag), treatment of right heart failure and iron deficiency, and continuation of calcium channel blockers in vasoresponders.

section_headings: 11.4.2. Treatment of venous thromboembolism in pregnancy
content.narrative_summary: Clinical signs and symptoms of pulmonary embolism (PE) in pregnancy are similar to non-pregnant women. To minimize computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA) use in stable suspected PE cases, diagnostic strategies combine clinical features, D-dimer measurement, and venous ultrasound. Although D-dimer rises physiologically during pregnancy (up to 39% in the third trimester), applying the YEARS criteria (clinical signs of acute DVT, haemoptysis, PE most likely diagnosis) with adjusted D-dimer thresholds (<500 µg/L if YEARS criteria present; <1000 µg/L if absent) plus peripheral venous compression ultrasound reduces CTPA need. A meta-analysis confirms inclusion of D-dimer refines diagnostic algorithms in pregnant women with suspected PE. In suspected VTE during pregnancy, therapeutic low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) should be started immediately, even before imaging, until VTE is excluded or confirmed. For confirmed acute VTE, weight-adjusted LMWH based on early pregnancy weight is recommended using either once- or twice-daily regimens to achieve a therapeutic daily dose; current evidence does not favour one regimen over the other.

Drug selection (oral nifedipine, labetalol, methyldopa) is based on diagnosis, pre‐eclampsia status, delivery timing, and physician preference; nifedipine may have superior efficacy and hydralazine is second‐line. Intravenous agents (labetalol, urapidil, nicardipine, nitroprusside) are used for acute control, and nitroglycerine infusion may be employed with diuretics. Section 12.3.4 reviews timing and mode of delivery in pre‐eclampsia, citing a trial that planned delivery within 48 h reduces maternal morbidity, recommends individualized delivery planning (around 39 weeks if well managed), continuous fetal monitoring for induction, neuraxial anaesthesia for severe cases, and advises stopping methyldopa within 2 days postpartum due to depression risk.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 13 — Recommendations for hypertensive disorders and pregnancy (see Evidence Tables 12–17)

rows.recommendation: It is recommended to aim for systolic BP <140 mmHg and diastolic BP <90 mmHg in pregnant women.
Systolic BP ≥160 mmHg or diastolic BP ≥110 mmHg in a pregnant woman is an emergency, and treatment in a hospital setting is recommended.

Low-dose aspirin (75–150 mg daily) is recommended in women at moderate or high risk of pre-eclampsia (i.e. at least one high-risk factor or two moderate-risk factors for pre-eclampsia) from weeks 12 to 36/37.
In women with gestational hypertension, initiation of drug treatment is recommended at systolic BP ≥140 mmHg or diastolic BP ≥90 mmHg.
Methyldopa is recommended for the treatment of hypertension in pregnancy.
Labetalol, metoprolol, and dihydropyridine CCBs are recommended for the treatment of hypertension in pregnancy.

In severe hypertension, drug treatment with i.v. labetalol, urapidil, nicardipine, or oral short acting nifedipine or methyldopa is recommended for acute reduction in blood pressure. Intravenous hydralazine is a second-line option.
In pre-eclampsia associated with pulmonary oedema, nitroglycerine given as an i.v. infusion is recommended.
In women with pre-eclampsia without severe features, delivery is recommended at 37 weeks.
It is recommended to expedite delivery in women with pre-eclampsia associated with adverse markers such as haemostatic disorders.
In women with gestational hypertension, delivery is recommended at 39 weeks.
Ambulatory BP or home BP monitoring should be considered to exclude white-coat and masked hypertension, which are common in pregnancy.
Home BP monitoring may be considered as an adjunct to office BP measurements in pregnant women to detect new-onset hypertension or for monitoring BP control.

content.title: 12.4. Arrhythmias
content.narrative_summary: The section describes that the incidence of arrhythmias in pregnant women is increasing due to older maternal age and cardiovascular risk factors such as obesity, hypertension, diabetes, and CAD. Physiological changes in hemodynamic, metabolic, hormonal, and autonomic function contribute to arrhythmogenesis, and women with a history of arrhythmia may experience worsening symptoms during pregnancy. Arrhythmias can adversely affect both mother and fetus and should be managed similarly to non-pregnant patients. For new-onset narrow QRS (<120 ms) supraventricular tachycardias in pregnancy, treatment is guided by hemodynamic stability: unstable cases (including AF and AFL) require synchronized direct-current cardioversion with fetal heart‐rate monitoring, while in stable cases vagal maneuvers (modified Valsalva, carotid sinus massage) can terminate AV(N)RT.

content.narrative_summary: The text continues the discussion of management of SVT in pregnant women, stating that if vagal manoeuvres fail, i.v. adenosine (6–18 mg bolus) is recommended to terminate AV(N)RT. Intravenous beta-1-selective blockers (preferably metoprolol) can be used for all SVTs, and non-dihydropyridine CCBs (verapamil) and digoxin may also be considered. In stable patients without structural heart disease, flecainide and ibutilide may be used; in congenital heart disease, synchronized direct current cardioversion is preferred. The section then introduces atrial fibrillation, noting its increasing incidence during pregnancy, associated risks, and that rapid conduction may have serious haemodynamic consequences. Direct current cardioversion is required for haemodynamically unstable AF with foetal monitoring, and rhythm control is preferred during pregnancy. Anti-arrhythmic drugs (e.g., flecainide and sotalol) are discussed, with sotalol requiring foetal growth monitoring. Limited data exist on propafenone; ibutilide or flecainide may be considered for AFL. Anticoagulation with LMWH before cardioversion or for transoesophageal echocardiography should be evaluated as in non-pregnant women and continued for at least four weeks post-cardioversion.

content.narrative_summary: The page continues management recommendations for supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) in pregnancy, then transitions to ventricular arrhythmias during pregnancy, noting that new-onset VT/VF are rare, idiopathic RVOT VT is most common, and underlying PPCM must be excluded. It recommends limiting amiodarone to life-threatening arrhythmias, using beta-blockers and other agents (flecainide, sotalol, quinidine) when indicated, and refers to Figure 16. It then outlines that electrical cardioversion is safe in all pregnancy phases with fetal monitoring and impedance similar to non-pregnant women, followed by advising catheter ablation after the first trimester in specialized centres.

content.title: 12.4.3.4. Implantable cardioverter defibrillator management
content.narrative_summary: Routine ICD interrogation and guidance are recommended prior to delivery for pregnant women with an ICD or pacemaker (see Figures 17 and 18). Women with structural heart disease are at higher risk of atrial and ventricular tachyarrhythmias during pregnancy and may present with inappropriate shocks due to lead defects, new-onset supraventricular tachyarrhythmias, or technical issues such as T-wave oversensing or noise sensing. Appropriate ICD shocks caused by ventricular tachyarrhythmias require exclusion of triggers (HF, electrolyte abnormalities, ischaemia, infection), with management including device reprogramming or adapting anti-arrhythmic drug therapy. In drug-refractory cases or serious anti-arrhythmic drug side effects, catheter ablation may be considered. Data indicate that maternal ICD shocks do not have major fetal adverse effects, and the approach to ICD shocks in pregnant women is similar to that in non-pregnant women. A wearable cardioverter-defibrillator may be considered when ICD implantation is indicated for reversible conditions.

figures_tables_algorithms.title: Management of pacemaker and implantable cardioverter defibrillator and pregnancy
figures_tables_algorithms.summary:
Algorithm outlining management across four phases:
- Pre-pregnancy: involve the Pregnancy Heart Team including an electrophysiologist in preparing pregnancy and delivery; initiate or adapt anti-arrhythmic drug therapy.
- Pregnancy: evaluate pacemaker/ICD function (battery status, sensing, pacing impedance; stored arrhythmia episodes); schedule regular follow-up visits.
- Admission for delivery:

  • ICD evaluation: adapt programming to minimize inappropriate shocks (VT therapy zone off, only VF zone on) OR place magnet over ICD battery to suspend therapy; for pacing-dependent women, use bipolar mode and avoid DOO/VOO programming.
- After delivery: reprogram pacemaker/ICD to original status.

content.title: 12.4.4. Cardiac arrest
content.narrative_summary: Maternal cardiac arrest occurs in 8/100 000 hospitalizations in the United States and 7.6/100 000 pregnancies in the Netherlands. Haemorrhage and anaesthetic complications are the most common overall causes of cardiac arrest, with heart failure, acute coronary syndromes, arrhythmias, aortic dissection, and pulmonary embolism the chief cardiovascular causes. Because most causes in pregnancy tend to be reversible, pregnant women have better outcomes than non-pregnant women. Basic cardiac arrest resuscitation principles apply, although beyond 20 weeks’ gestation left lateral manual displacement of the uterus or left lateral positioning is indicated to avoid aortocaval compression. Chest compressions should follow standard basic life support guidelines.

Maternal interventions are divided into not pregnancy-specific (airway management; drug choices and doses as in non-pregnant (Class I); chest compressions as in non-pregnant (Class I); defibrillation protocol as in non-pregnant (Class I); anterolateral defibrillator pad placement under the breast (Class I)) and pregnancy-specific (continuous manual left uterine displacement (Class I); i.v. access above diaphragm (Class I); in women receiving Mg++ infusion (pre-eclampsia): stop Mg++ and administer calcium gluconate; temperature control on individual basis in resuscitated pregnant women). Obstetric interventions: if no ROSC after 4 min and fetus is viable, immediate caesarean section (Class IIa); neonatal team activation.

section_headings: 12.4.5.3. Management of sinus node dysfunction and atrioventricular block
content.narrative_summary: The page continues guidance on post–cardiac arrest care in pregnancy, recommending full left lateral decubitus positioning, avoidance of device-assisted compressions due to lack of data, no withholding of drugs over teratogenicity concerns, mandatory fetal monitoring, and preparation for emergency caesarean or rapid maternal transfer. It then addresses bradycardia: sinus node dysfunction is rare and may present as hypotension; management depends on cause and risks. Mobitz type I AV block is common and usually benign; pacemaker placement is individualized. In life-threatening bradycardia, treat as in non-pregnancy, with isoproterenol and pacing per standard indications; pacemakers can be safely implanted with minimal fluoroscopy. The section on valvular heart disease notes congenital or rheumatic origins, pregnancy complications (new-onset AF, thromboembolism, heart failure), need for preconception counseling and optimization, and that stenotic lesions limit cardiac output with symptomatic presentation in pregnancy and up to 50% increase in valve gradients on serial echocardiography.

content.narrative_summary: Section 12.5.3 addresses prosthetic valves in women of childbearing age, emphasizing the need to consider future pregnancies when choosing valve type. Bioprosthetic valves or valve repair are preferred to avoid anticoagulation, with data from the ROPAC III and M-PAC registries showing varying live birth rates (54% for mechanical heart valves vs 79% for tissue valves) and major adverse cardiovascular event rates (40% vs 34%). The Ross procedure is noted as an alternative with low pregnancy risk. Transcatheter valve-in-valve interventions may extend bioprosthetic valve lifespan, as described in the CARPREG data. Section 12.5.3.2 introduces mechanical valves, highlighting high complication and bleeding risks in pregnancy and the importance of comprehensive pre-pregnancy planning and anticoagulation strategy.

content.narrative_summary: Infective endocarditis during pregnancy is rare but carries significant maternal and fetal morbidity and mortality, most commonly caused by Staphylococcus and Serratia species, with highest mortality in delivery subgroup; antibiotic prophylaxis should follow standard guidelines based on cultures and toxicities. Heart failure complicates approximately 11% of pregnancies, with a 9% in-hospital maternal mortality; pre-pregnancy counseling, risk stratification, and regular reassessment are required, and patients with severe pre-existing or de novo acute heart failure (including cardiogenic shock) need expert care, inotropic support, possible mechanical circulatory support, and consideration of delivery timing.

rows.recommendation: It is recommended that women with HFrEF are advised about the risk of deterioration of cardiac function during pregnancy and peripartum.
In pregnant women with HFrEF, it is recommended that non-selective beta-blockers are switched to beta-1-selective blockers (metoprolol, bisoprolol) with close maternal and foetal monitoring.
Anticoagulation with therapeutic doses of LMWH is recommended in pregnant women with intracardiac thrombus or decreased LV function with EF <35%.
It is recommended to optimize HF guideline-directed medical therapy after delivery, taking contraindicated drugs during lactation into account.
Due to the high metabolic demands of lactation, avoiding lactation may be considered in women with severe HF.
ACE-Is, ARBs, ARNIs, MRAs, ivabradine, and SGLT2 inhibitors are not recommended during pregnancy due to adverse foetal effects.
Inotropes and/or vasopressors are recommended in pregnant women with cardiogenic shock with levosimendan, dobutamine, and milrinone as recommended agents.

Urgent delivery with caesarean section is recommended in pregnant women with cardiogenic shock as soon as the foetus is viable, taking gestational age, comorbidities, and the available level of medical care into account.
Early transfer of pregnant women in cardiogenic shock to a facility providing mechanical circulatory support should be considered.
Preventing lactation may be considered in women with severe HF due to the high metabolic demands of lactation.

figures_tables_algorithms.label: Figure 22
figures_tables_algorithms.title: Management of acute heart failure and cardiogenic shock in pregnancy and up to 6 months post-partum
figures_tables_algorithms.summary: Flowchart outlining management of acute heart failure (HF) and cardiogenic shock in pregnancy and up to 6 months postpartum. Initial steps include considering corticosteroids for fetal lung maturation before 35 weeks and assessing HF severity. For severe HF or cardiogenic shock: optimize preload (volume vs diuretics; initiate nitrates if SBP >110 mmHg) and oxygenation (non-invasive or invasive ventilation if SpO₂ <95%), add inotropes/vasopressors (levosimendan without loading dose, dobutamine, or milrinone; Class I), urgent caesarean delivery in cardiogenic shock (Class I), then mechanical circulatory support (VA-ECMO or LVAD) as bridge-to-recovery or bridge-to-bridge if refractory, and heart transplantation if no recovery. For no severe HF or shock, management depends on delivery status: if delivered, start ACE-I/ARB/ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2-i, diuretics (Class I), consider ivabradine; in peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM), bromocriptine (Class IIb) and anticoagulation with heparin/LMWH (Class IIa). If not delivered, use hydralazine, nitrates, beta-blocker (bisoprolol, metoprolol succinate), diuretics; avoid ACE-I/ARB/ARNI/MRA/ivabradine/SGLT2-i (Class III); consider vaginal delivery with epidural analgesia (Class I).

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 21 — Recommendations for heart transplantation and pregnancy

rows.recommendation: It is recommended to postpone pregnancy until at least 1 year after heart transplantation, taking individual risk factors into account.

In women with a heart transplant, it is recommended that immunosuppression serum drug levels are monitored during pregnancy every 4 weeks until the 32nd week, then every 2 weeks until the 36th week, then weekly until delivery, and for 6–12 months after delivery to guide dosing.
It is recommended to perform weekly monitoring of donor-specific antibodies for at least 6–12 months after delivery.
Paternal HLA testing prior to conception should be considered due to the risk of developing donor-specific antibodies.
Mycophenolic acid therapy is not recommended in pregnancy and should be discontinued 6 weeks before conception.

Cardiac troponin and NP measurements may be considered at baseline and during anthracycline chemotherapy in pregnant women with cancer.

content.narrative_summary: Key messages include involvement of a Pregnancy Heart Team for women with mWHO 2.0 class II–III heart disease from pre-conception through late postpartum, with detailed delivery planning; complete pre-pregnancy re-evaluation and optimisation of treatment in known CVD; structured psychosocial support; counselling on heritable cardiovascular transmission risks and assisted reproductive options; individualised, shared decision-making respecting maternal autonomy; comprehensive counselling for mWHO class IV and preference for vaginal delivery; life-threatening treatments mirroring non-pregnant care; cautious use of non-invasive imaging with ionizing radiation only when benefit outweighs risk; continuation and monitoring of beta-blockers in LQTS and CPVT (atenolol contraindicated); full post-partum beta-blocker dosing in LQT2; consideration of genetic testing in PPCM and aortic disease management guided by P/LP variants; expert counselling for ACHD lesions by a Pregnancy Heart Team with shared decision-making; and recognition that no safe pulmonary artery pressure cut-off has been established in pregnancy.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 23 — Recommendations for long-term effects of adverse pregnancy outcomes

rows.recommendation: It is recommended to undertake a cardiovascular risk assessment in women with APOs, to recognize and document APOs when CVD risk is evaluated in women, and to provide counselling on the importance of healthy lifestyle choices that optimize cardiovascular health.

In women with persistent post-partum hypertension beyond 6 weeks to 3 months post-partum, initiation of antihypertensive therapy with reference to lactating status is recommended following current guidelines.
In cases where adoption of healthy lifestyle choices alone is inadequate to control post-partum glucose levels, initiation of pharmacotherapy following current guidelines is recommended.
It is recommended that women with a history of GDM undergo a formal oGTT 6–12 weeks post-partum with a repeat assessment at 6–12 months and regular annual follow-up visits to screen for diabetes.
Nifedipine and labetalol (metoprolol if labetalol is unavailable) are recommended as treatments for uncomplicated post-partum hypertension in the first 6 weeks after delivery.

In women with a history of any APO, cardiovascular risk assessment should be considered at 3 months post-partum with repeat assessment at 6–12 months after implementation of appropriate lifestyle interventions, and regular long-term follow-up thereafter.
Breastfeeding may be considered in order to lower the future cardiovascular risk in women with APOs.

recommendation_tables.title: Table 16 ‘What to do’ and ‘what not to do’

rows.recommendation: It is recommended to perform a risk assessment in all women with CVD of childbearing age using the mWHO 2.0 classification.

A discussion by the Pregnancy Heart Team about the high risk of maternal mortality or morbidity and the related high foetal risk is recommended for women with mWHO 2.0 class IV CVD conditions, including a shared decision-making process for pregnancy termination, involving psychological support.
It is recommended that women with CVD of mWHO 2.0 class II–III and above are evaluated and managed by a Pregnancy Heart Team from pre-pregnancy onwards through pregnancy and post-partum.

It is recommended that women with CVD of mWHO 2.0 class II and above, or those at risk of developing CVD, receive individualized advice to determine the most suitable contraception method, including emergency contraception.

Assessment by a clinical geneticist prior to pregnancy is recommended in women fulfilling diagnostic criteria for inherited cardiovascular disease to guide risk stratification and pre-natal genetic testing.

Pre-conception genetic counselling is recommended in couples with heritable CVD, whether genetic testing is being considered or not. It is recommended that this counselling is provided by an appropriately trained healthcare professional within a multidisciplinary team that offers psychological support and education to encourage decision-making.
It is recommended that single embryo transfer is performed in women with CVD.
It is recommended to offer women with CVD access to termination of pregnancy that is tailored to their cardiac condition to minimize the risks of the procedure.
Transthoracic echocardiography is recommended as first-line imaging tool in any pregnant woman with unexplained or new cardiovascular signs or symptoms.
It is recommended to limit exposure to all medical ionizing radiation doses to ALARA levels.
It is recommended to keep the radiation dose to the foetus as low as possible (preferably <50 mGy), particularly if the foetus is in the field of view.
Vaginal delivery is recommended in most women with CVD.
Routine induction of labour prior to 39 weeks is not recommended in women with stable CVD.
It is recommended that the timing of delivery is planned to ensure safe and effective peripartum anticoagulation.
It is recommended to discontinue VKAs and start therapeutic-dose LMWH or adjusted-dose i.v. UFH at the 36th week of gestation or 2 weeks before the planned delivery.
In women at low risk on therapeutic-dose LMWH, neuraxial anaesthesia and vaginal delivery (or caesarean section for obstetric indications) is recommended 24 h after the last dose of LMWH.

In women at high risk, it is recommended to convert LMWH to i.v. UFH at least 36 h prior to delivery and stop the UFH infusion 4–6 h prior to anticipated delivery. The aPTT should be normal before regional anaesthesia.
If delivery starts while the mother is on VKAs or <2 weeks after discontinuation of VKAs, caesarean section is recommended for foetal protection.
Post-delivery, it is recommended that the decision to restart LMWH or UFH is made after discussion with the Pregnancy Heart Team and the woman who gave birth.

section_headings: 6. Pregnancy in women with cardiomyopathies and primary arrhythmia syndromes
content.narrative_summary: This page provides a series of tabulated recommendations on drug management during pregnancy and lactation, cardiomyopathies and arrhythmia syndromes in pregnancy, peripartum cardiomyopathy counselling, and aortopathies in pregnancy.

rows.recommendation: It is recommended to postpone the switch from heparin back to oral anticoagulants until 7–14 days post-partum when the wound area has healed, in consultation with the Pregnancy Heart Team.

recommendation_tables.title: Direct oral anticoagulants and pregnancy

rows.recommendation: DOACs are not recommended during pregnancy.

recommendation_tables.title: Cardiomyopathies and pregnancy

rows.recommendation: Clinical cardiological surveillance (ECG, echocardiogram, and Holter ECG monitoring) is recommended during pregnancy in women with CMPs, depending on individual risk.

Vaginal delivery is recommended in most women with CMPs, unless there are obstetric indications for caesarean section, severe HF (EF <30% and/or NYHA class III/IV), uncontrolled arrhythmias, or severe outflow obstruction (≥50 mmHg) in women with HCM, or in women presenting in labour on VKAs.
In women with DCM and worsening of EF during pregnancy, counselling on the risk of recurrence during a subsequent pregnancy is recommended in all cases, even after recovery of LV function.
It is recommended to use the same risk stratification protocol for ventricular arrhythmias in pregnant women with HCM as for non-pregnant women with HCM.
It is recommended to start beta-blockers in women with HCM who develop symptoms due to outflow tract obstruction or arrhythmia during pregnancy.

It is recommended that women with HCM with symptomatic LV dysfunction (EF <50%) and/or severe LVOTO (≥50 mmHg) wishing to become pregnant are counselled by the Pregnancy Heart Team regarding the high risk of pregnancy-related adverse events.
Myosin inhibitors are not recommended in women during pregnancy due to lack of safety data.

recommendation_tables.title: Primary arrhythmia syndromes and pregnancy

rows.recommendation: Monitoring and treatment of hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia is recommended in pregnant women with primary arrhythmia syndromes suffering from hyperemesis.
Beta-blockers, with pre-pregnancy dose and with nadolol and propranolol as drugs of choice, are recommended during pregnancy in women with LQTS.
It is recommended to continue beta-blocker therapy during lactation in women with LQTS to reduce arrhythmic risk.

Pre-pregnancy dose beta-blocker of nadolol or propranolol are recommended in women with LQT2, particularly in the post-partum period, which represents a high-risk period for life-threatening arrhythmias.
Beta-blockers, with pre-pregnancy dose and with nadolol and propranolol as drugs of choice, are recommended during pregnancy and lactation in women with CPVT.
Flecainide, in addition to beta-blockers, is recommended in women with CPVT who experience cardiac events such as syncope, VT, or cardiac arrest, during pregnancy.

It is recommended that women with CPVT who are stable on beta-blockers (nadolol or propranolol as drugs of choice) and flecainide before pregnancy, continue both drugs also during pregnancy and post-partum.

recommendation_tables.title: Peripartum cardiomyopathy

rows.recommendation: Counselling for women with PPCM about the risk of recurrence during a subsequent pregnancy and about contraception is recommended in all cases, even after recovery of LV function (LVEF >50%).

recommendation_tables.title: Pregnancy in women with aortopathies

rows.recommendation: It is recommended that women with aortic disease have counselling about the risk of aortic dissection in pregnancy and the post-partum period.

It is recommended that women with a history of aortic dissection or -surgery have pre-pregnancy counselling about the high risk by an extended Pregnancy Heart Team considering the presence and type of genetic variant, aortic morphology, growth rate, and aetiology of aortic dissection.

It is recommended that women with vascular Ehlers–Danlos syndrome wishing to become pregnant are counselled regarding the very high risk of pregnancy-related adverse events by a multidisciplinary team, considering family history, genetic variant, and previous vascular events.
Imaging of the entire aorta (CT or CMR) is recommended before pregnancy in women with known or suspected aortic disease.

In women with aortic dilatation related to BAV, imaging (with TTE, and CMR/CT if needed) of the aortic root, ascending aorta, and descending aorta (to rule out coarctation) is recommended before pregnancy.
In women with low-risk aortic disease (mWHO 2.0 classes II and II–III), one-time echocardiographic imaging between 20 and 30 weeks of gestation and imaging at 6 months post-partum is recommended.

rows.recommendation: In women with moderate to high-risk aortic disease (mWHO 2.0 classes III and IV), repeated echocardiographic imaging every 4–12 weeks (depending on diagnosis and severity of dilatation) is recommended during pregnancy and until 6 months post-partum.
CMR (without gadolinium) imaging of the entire aorta is recommended in pregnant women at risk of or with known aortic dilatation who have not had recent pre-pregnancy cross-sectional imaging.
It is recommended that centres managing pregnancies in women with moderate to high-risk aortic disease (mWHO 2.0 class III/IV) can provide cardiovascular surgery in case of peripartum adverse events.
When a woman with known aortic dilatation, history of dissection, or P/LP variant associated with aortic disease becomes pregnant, strict and individualized BP control is recommended.
Beta-blocker therapy throughout pregnancy and in the post-partum period is recommended in women with MFS and other HTADs.
Celiprolol is recommended in women with vascular Ehlers–Danlos syndrome during pregnancy and lactation.

It is recommended that indications for pre-pregnancy aortic root and/or ascending aortic surgery are guided by aortic morphology, underlying pathology, family history, genetic variant, previous vascular events, and patient’s preference.
In women with MFS and aortic root diameters >45 mm, surgery before pregnancy is recommended.
In women with LDS with P/LP variants in TGFBR1, TGFBR2, and aortic root diameters ≥45 mm, surgery before pregnancy is recommended.
In women with nsHTAD with P/LP variants in MYH11, ACTA2, PRKG1, or MYLK, and aortic root diameters ≥45 mm, surgery before pregnancy is recommended.
In women with BAV and aortic root or ascending aortic diameter ≥50 mm, surgery before pregnancy is recommended.
In women without an identifiable P/LP variant with aortic root or ascending aortic diameters ≥50 mm, surgery before pregnancy is recommended.
In women with an aorta <40 mm, vaginal delivery is recommended.
In women with vascular Ehlers–Danlos syndrome, caesarean section at 37 weeks is recommended for obstetrical reasons.
The use of ergometrine post-delivery is not recommended in women with aortopathy.

recommendation_tables.title: 9. Pregnancy in women with known congenital heart disease

rows.recommendation: Vaginal delivery is recommended in most women with ACHD.
It is recommended that all women with Fontan circulation who wish to become pregnant receive counselling from the Pregnancy Heart Team regarding the high risk of pregnancy-related adverse events.

It is recommended that women with a systemic RV (Mustard/Senning or congenitally corrected TGA), in NYHA class III/IV, systemic ventricular dysfunction (EF <40%), or severe TR wishing to become pregnant are counselled by the Pregnancy Heart Team regarding the high risk of pregnancy-related adverse events.
In women with significant haemodynamic lesions, discussion about guideline-directed interventions is recommended prior to pregnancy.

recommendation_tables.title: 10. Pregnancy in women with pulmonary arterial hypertension

rows.recommendation: It is recommended that women of childbearing potential with PAH wishing to become pregnant are counselled by a multidisciplinary team regarding the very high risk of pregnancy-related adverse events, encouraging a shared decision-making process about whether to become pregnant.
It is recommended to provide clear contraceptive advice to women of childbearing potential with PAH.
For women with PAH requiring pregnancy termination, it is recommended to perform this in PH centres.
Endothelin receptor antagonists, riociguat, and selexipag are not recommended during pregnancy.

recommendation_tables.title: 11. Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy and post-partum

rows.recommendation: For pregnant or post-partum women at high risk of VTE, a prophylactic fixed dose of LMWH is recommended over a higher weight-adjusted dose to reduce the risk of VTE.

In pregnant women or women in the post-partum period with suspicion of VTE (DVT and/or PE), an immediate formal diagnostic assessment with validated methods is recommended and should not be postponed.

In pregnant women or women in the post-partum period with newly diagnosed VTE (DVT and/or PE), the involvement of the Pregnancy Heart Team, including a vascular specialist and a haematologist, is recommended.
In pregnant or post-partum women with a diagnosis of VTE without haemodynamic instability, anticoagulation is recommended by using therapeutic-dose LMWH based on early pregnancy body weight.

recommendation_tables.title: 12. Pregnancy in women with acquired heart disease

rows.recommendation: In pregnant women with chest pain, it is recommended to exclude life-threatening cardiovascular conditions, including PE, ACS (including SCAD), and acute aortic syndrome.

section_headings: Ventricular tachycardia, device implantation, catheter ablation, and pregnancy
content.narrative_summary: Page provides Class I and Class III recommendations on the management of acute coronary syndrome, hypertensive disorders, supraventricular and ventricular tachycardias, device implantation, catheter ablation, cardiac arrest, congenital AV block, and native valve disease in pregnant women.

recommendation_tables.title: Acute coronary syndrome and pregnancy

rows.recommendation: It is recommended to manage pregnant women with ACS in the same way as non-pregnant women, including diagnostic investigations and interventions.
Low-dose ASA is recommended as the antiplatelet treatment of choice during pregnancy and lactation when single antiplatelet treatment is indicated.
If DAPT is required, clopidogrel is recommended as the P2Y12 inhibitor of choice during pregnancy.

The duration of DAPT (aspirin and clopidogrel) in pregnant women undergoing coronary stent implantation is recommended to be the same as in non-pregnant women, with an individual approach considering ischaemic risk and delivery-related bleeding risks.

recommendation_tables.title: Hypertensive disorders and pregnancy

rows.recommendation: It is recommended to aim for systolic BP <140 mmHg and diastolic BP <90 mmHg in pregnant women.
Systolic BP ≥160 mmHg or diastolic BP ≥110 mmHg in a pregnant woman is an emergency, and treatment in a hospital setting is recommended.

Low-dose aspirin (75–150 mg daily) is recommended in women at moderate or high risk of pre-eclampsia (i.e. at least one high risk factor or two moderate risk factors for pre-eclampsia) from weeks 12 to 36/37.
In women with gestational hypertension, initiation of drug treatment is recommended at systolic BP ≥140 mmHg or diastolic BP ≥90 mmHg.
Methyldopa is recommended for the treatment of hypertension in pregnancy.
Labetalol, metoprolol, and dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are recommended for the treatment of hypertension in pregnancy.

In severe hypertension, drug treatment with i.v. labetalol, urapidil, nicardipine, or oral short-acting nifedipine or methyldopa is recommended for acute reduction in blood pressure. Intravenous hydralazine is a second-line option.
In pre-eclampsia associated with pulmonary oedema, nitroglycerine given as an i.v. infusion is recommended.
In women with pre-eclampsia without severe features, delivery is recommended at 37 weeks.
It is recommended to expedite delivery in women with pre-eclampsia associated with adverse markers such as haemostatic disorders.
In women with gestational hypertension, delivery is recommended at 39 weeks.

recommendation_tables.title: Supraventricular tachycardia and pregnancy

rows.recommendation: Immediate electrical cardioversion is recommended for acute treatment of SVT with haemodynamic instability.
Vagal manoeuvres and i.v. adenosine are recommended for conversion of haemodynamically stable supraventricular tachycardias.
Intravenous beta-blockers (metoprolol) are recommended as the first-line option for acute rate control in pregnant women with AF or AF with preserved LVEF and rapid ventricular rate.
Therapeutic anticoagulation with LMWH is recommended for pregnant women with persistent or permanent AF at elevated thromboembolic risk.
Beta-1-selective blockers are recommended for rate control in pregnant women with AF, AFL, or FAT.
Beta-1-selective blockers or verapamil are recommended for the prevention of SVT in women without pre-excitation on resting ECG.
Flecainide or propafenone are recommended for the prevention of arrhythmias in pregnant women with WPW syndrome.

recommendation_tables.title: Ventricular tachycardia, device implantation, catheter ablation, and pregnancy

rows.recommendation: Immediate electrical cardioversion is recommended for both unstable and stable ventricular tachycardias.
Beta-blockers or verapamil are recommended for the prevention of idiopathic sustained VT.
If an ICD, pacemaker, or resynchronization therapy device is indicated during pregnancy, implantation is recommended with optimal radiation protection.

recommendation_tables.title: Cardiac arrest and pregnancy

rows.recommendation: Continuous manual left uterine displacement during CPR in pregnant women (≥20 weeks) with cardiac arrest is recommended to relieve aortocaval compression.
It is recommended to establish i.v. access above the diaphragm to ensure that the i.v. therapy is not obstructed by the gravid uterus.
It is recommended to perform the same chest compressions and defibrillation protocols in pregnant as in non-pregnant women.
Anterolateral defibrillator pad placement is recommended with the lateral pad placed under the breast.
It is recommended that no drugs are withheld in pregnant women with cardiac arrest due to concerns of teratogenicity.

recommendation_tables.title: Congenital atrioventricular block and pregnancy

rows.recommendation: In pregnant women with asymptomatic congenital AV block, normal cardiac anatomy and function, a narrow QRS complex, and ventricular rate (≥50 b.p.m.), a prophylactic temporary pacemaker during delivery is not recommended.

recommendation_tables.title: Native valve disease and pregnancy

rows.recommendation: Intervention is recommended before pregnancy in symptomatic patients with severe aortic stenosis.
Intervention is recommended before pregnancy in women with mitral stenosis and a valve area <1.5 cm².

13. Long-term effects of adverse pregnancy outcomes

rows.recommendation: In pregnant women with symptomatic mitral stenosis or pulmonary hypertension, restricted activities and beta-blockers are recommended.
In pregnant women with mitral stenosis, diuretics are recommended when congestive symptoms persist despite beta-blockers.
Full therapeutic-dose anticoagulation is recommended in women with mitral stenosis complicated by AF, left atrial thrombus, or prior embolism.
Surgical treatment is recommended before pregnancy in women with severe aortic or mitral regurgitation with symptoms, impaired ventricular function, or marked ventricular dilatation.
Diuretics are recommended in pregnant women with regurgitant lesions when symptoms or signs of congestion occur.

recommendation_tables.title: Prosthetic valves and pregnancy

rows.recommendation: A bioprosthetic valve is recommended (over a mechanical valve) in young women contemplating pregnancy requiring a valve prosthesis.
It is recommended that the type of valve surgery or intervention for a woman contemplating pregnancy is chosen in consultation with the Pregnancy Heart Team.

It is recommended that a care plan documenting the agreed anticoagulant strategy (including the decision to continue VKAs or converting to therapeutic-dose LMWH in the first trimester) is in place for women of childbearing age with an MHV prior to pregnancy or as soon as pregnancy is recognized.
It is recommended that pregnant women with an MHV are managed by the Pregnancy Heart Team.
In pregnant women on VKAs, it is recommended to perform INR monitoring weekly or at a minimum every 2 weeks.
In pregnant women with MHVs on therapeutic-dose LMWH, it is recommended to check peak anti-factor Xa levels and to target levels according to individualized risk.
LMWH is not recommended when anti-factor Xa level monitoring is not available.

recommendation_tables.title: Chronic and acute heart failure and pregnancy

rows.recommendation: It is recommended that women with HFrEF are advised about the risk of deterioration of cardiac function during pregnancy and peripartum.
In pregnant women with HFrEF, it is recommended that non-selective beta-blockers are switched to beta-1-selective blockers (metoprolol, bisoprolol) with close maternal and foetal monitoring.
Anticoagulation with therapeutic doses of LMWH is recommended in pregnant women with intracardiac thrombus or decreased LV function with EF <35%.
It is recommended to optimize HF guideline-directed medical therapy after delivery, taking contraindicated drugs during lactation into account.

Urgent delivery with caesarean section is recommended in pregnant women with cardiogenic shock as soon as the foetus is viable, taking gestational age, comorbidities, and the available level of medical care into account.
Inotropes and/or vasopressors are recommended in pregnant women with cardiogenic shock with levosimendan, dobutamine, and milrinone as recommended agents.
ACE-Is, ARBs, ARNIs, MRAs, ivabradine, and SGLT2 inhibitors are not recommended during pregnancy due to adverse foetal effects.

recommendation_tables.title: Heart transplantation and pregnancy

rows.recommendation: It is recommended to postpone pregnancy until at least 1 year after heart transplantation, taking individual risk factors into account.

In women with a heart transplant, it is recommended that immunosuppression serum drug levels are monitored during pregnancy every 4 weeks until the 32nd week, then every 2 weeks until the 36th week, then weekly until delivery, and for 6–12 months after delivery to guide dosing.
It is recommended to perform weekly monitoring of donor-specific antibodies for at least 6–12 months after delivery.

rows.recommendation: It is recommended to undertake a cardiovascular risk assessment in women with APOs, to recognize and document APOs when CVD risk is evaluated in women, and to provide counselling on the importance of healthy lifestyle choices that optimize cardiovascular health.

In women with persistent post-partum hypertension beyond 6 weeks to 3 months post-partum, initiation of antihypertensive therapy with reference to lactating status is recommended following current guidelines.
In cases where adoption of healthy lifestyle choices alone is inadequate to control post-partum glucose levels, initiation of pharmacotherapy following current guidelines is recommended.
It is recommended that women with a history of GDM undergo a formal oGTT 6–12 weeks post-partum with a repeat assessment at 6–12 months and regular annual follow-up visits to screen for diabetes.
